overview.title: Max pooling vs. a ConvNet without pooling
overview.main_topic: What max pooling does, how it differs from convolution, and a counter-example model (Listing 8.5) that omits max pooling
overview.central_idea: Max pooling extracts small windows (usually 2 × 2, stride 2) and keeps the per-channel maximum, halving the spatial size. To show why this downsampling matters, the authors build a ConvNet with three stacked convolutions and no pooling, and start listing what goes wrong with it.
overview.importance: This page gives the mechanical definition of max pooling and sets up the argument for why ConvNets alternate convolution and pooling. That pattern comes back in every ConvNet in the book (p.269, p.304).
learning_objectives: Define max pooling as a per-channel max over local windows, and compare it with convolution's learned linear transform of patches
Know the usual hyperparameters: 2 × 2 windows with stride 2 for pooling, 3 × 3 windows with stride 1 for convolution
Read the model summary of Listing 8.5 and derive every output shape and parameter count
Explain the first problem of a pooling-free ConvNet: receptive fields grow too slowly to build a spatial hierarchy
prerequisites: The convolution operation, feature maps, filters and kernel size (section 8.1.1, p.258 onward)
Border effects and valid padding: a 3 × 3 valid convolution shrinks each spatial dimension by 2 (p.262-263)
The Keras functional API (keras.Input, calling layers on tensors, keras.Model)

summary:
This page continues section 8.1.2. The authors first define **max pooling**: windows are extracted from the input feature maps and the **maximum value of each channel** in each window is output. This is *conceptually similar to convolution*. Both work on local patches. The difference is that convolution transforms each patch with a **learned linear transformation** (the kernel), while max pooling applies a **hardcoded `max` operation** with no trainable weights. The two also differ in their usual settings. Max pooling typically uses **2 × 2 windows with stride 2**, which downsamples the feature maps by a factor of 2. Convolution typically uses **3 × 3 windows with no stride (stride 1)**.

The authors then ask why we downsample at all. Why not drop pooling and keep large feature maps throughout? To find out, **Listing 8.5** builds an "incorrectly structured" ConvNet. It has three `Conv2D` layers (64, 128 and 256 filters, kernel size 3, ReLU) applied to 28 × 28 × 1 MNIST inputs, followed by `GlobalAveragePooling2D` and a 10-way softmax `Dense` layer. The `summary()` output shows the spatial size shrinking only by the border effect, 28 → 26 → 24 → 22, while the channels grow to 256. The model has 372,234 parameters in total, almost all of them in the convolution layers.

The page ends by asking "What's wrong with this setup?" and starts the first of two answers. The model is not conducive to learning a **spatial hierarchy of features**, because the 3 × 3 windows of the third layer only contain information from 7 × 7 windows of the input. That sentence, and the second problem (a huge 22 × 22 final feature map that global average pooling then crushes), continue on p.265.

paragraphs.excerpt: Max pooling consists of extracting windows from the input feature maps and outputting
paragraphs.what_it_says: Max pooling extracts windows from the input feature maps and outputs the maximum of each channel within each window. It is conceptually like convolution, but patches are transformed by a hardcoded `max` instead of a learned linear transformation (the kernel). Max pooling usually uses 2 × 2 windows with stride 2, halving the feature maps. Convolution typically uses 3 × 3 windows with stride 1.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Pooling is a fixed, parameter-free local summary. It works **independently per channel**: channel 5 of the output is the max of channel 5 over the window, and channels never mix. A convolution, by contrast, mixes all input channels through its kernel. Because the pooling windows do not overlap (window size = stride = 2), each output position summarizes a distinct 2 × 2 block, so height and width are both halved (26 × 26 → 13 × 13, as p.263 noted). A stride-1 convolution moves one pixel at a time, so the windows overlap and only the border effect shrinks the output.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This contrast explains the division of labour in a classic ConvNet: convolutions *detect* patterns densely, and pooling *downsamples* by keeping the strongest response in each neighbourhood. It also explains why pooling layers show 0 parameters in model summaries.
paragraphs.technical_idea: For a 2 × 2 window and stride 2: $y_{i,j,c} = \max_{0\le a,b\le 1} x_{2i+a,\,2j+b,\,c}$. Output size is $\lfloor H/2 \rfloor \times \lfloor W/2 \rfloor \times C$, with the channel count unchanged.

The local spatial patch (e.g. 2 × 2) considered at one output position.
Distance between successive windows; stride 2 with 2 × 2 windows gives non-overlapping tiles and halves resolution.
Reduce the spatial resolution (height and width) of a feature map.

paragraphs.excerpt: Why downsample feature maps this way? Why not remove the max-pooling layers
paragraphs.what_it_says: The authors ask why we should downsample feature maps this way, and why we shouldn't remove the max-pooling layers and keep fairly large feature maps all the way up. They propose to look at this option, and say the model would then look like the following listing.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is an argument by counter-example. Instead of claiming abstractly that pooling helps, the authors build the alternative and examine what it lacks. Keeping "large feature maps all the way up" means letting only the valid-padding border effect reduce spatial size.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This reasoning carries over to architecture design in general: every component should be justifiable by what breaks without it. The same question returns in chapter 11, where max pooling is deliberately replaced by strided convolutions (p.339).

paragraphs.what_it_says: The authors announce that there are two problems with the pooling-free model.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This sentence introduces the two-bullet critique. Only the first bullet starts on this page; the second is on p.265.

paragraphs.excerpt: It isn’t conducive to learning a spatial hierarchy of features. The 3
paragraphs.what_it_says: First problem: the setup isn't conducive to learning a spatial hierarchy of features. The 3 × 3 windows in the third layer only contain information coming from 7 × 7 windows in the initial input (the sentence ends on p.265).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each stride-1 3 × 3 convolution grows the **receptive field** by 2 pixels: layer 1 sees 3 × 3 of the input, layer 2 sees 5 × 5, layer 3 sees 7 × 7. A 7 × 7 patch is a small part of a 28 × 28 digit, so even the deepest features are still local. Pooling would multiply this growth: after a 2 × 2 pooling, each later pixel stands for a 2 × 2 block of the previous map, so the next 3 × 3 convolution covers roughly twice the input extent.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The premise of ConvNets (p.257) is that later layers combine small patterns into larger, more abstract ones. If the receptive field never grows beyond a small patch, that hierarchy cannot form, however many channels the layers have.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Receptive field of $L$ stacked stride-1 $k\times k$ convs: $r_L = 1 + L(k-1)$, so for $k=3$, $L=3$: $r=7$.

terminology.meaning: Organization in which early layers detect small local patterns (edges) and later layers combine them into larger patterns (shapes, objects).
The region of the original input that can influence a given unit of a feature map.

connections: p.265: the bullet continues ('try recognizing a digit by only looking at it through windows that are 7 × 7 pixels!')
p.257: ConvNets learn spatial hierarchies of patterns

concepts.name: Max pooling
concepts.definition: An operation that slides (usually non-overlapping) windows over a feature map and outputs, for each channel separately, the maximum value inside each window.
concepts.intuition: It keeps the strongest response in each small neighbourhood: "was this feature present anywhere in this 2 × 2 tile, and how strongly?"
concepts.technical: With pool size 2 and stride 2, (H, W, C) → (⌊H/2⌋, ⌊W/2⌋, C). There are no trainable weights. During backprop the gradient flows only to the argmax position of each window.
concepts.significance: It is the standard downsampling step in classification ConvNets. It shrinks feature maps and helps later convolutions see larger parts of the input.
concepts.example: A 2 × 2 window [[1, 3], [0, 2]] in one channel becomes 3.
concepts.misconception: Max pooling does not mix channels and does not learn anything; it is not a smaller convolution.

concepts.name: Convolution (contrast)
concepts.definition: Transforms each local patch through a learned linear transformation (the kernel) shared across positions.
concepts.intuition: A learned pattern detector applied everywhere in the image.
concepts.technical: Typically 3 × 3 windows, stride 1. With valid padding, each spatial dimension shrinks by k − 1 = 2. All input channels are mixed into each output channel.
concepts.significance: Convolution provides the learned features; pooling provides the downsampling.
concepts.misconception: A stride-1 convolution does not meaningfully reduce resolution; it only loses the borders.

concepts.name: Spatial hierarchy of features
concepts.definition: The arrangement in which successive layers detect increasingly large and abstract patterns.
concepts.technical: It requires the receptive field of deep units to cover a large fraction of the input. Downsampling between conv layers makes receptive fields grow multiplicatively rather than additively.
concepts.significance: The authors give the lack of it as the first defect of the pooling-free model.
concepts.example: Without pooling, three 3 × 3 convs only reach 7 × 7 of a 28 × 28 image.
concepts.misconception: Adding more filters (64 → 128 → 256) does not enlarge what each unit can see.

concepts.name: Receptive field
concepts.definition: The region of the input image that influences a given unit.
concepts.intuition: How much of the picture a neuron can "see".
concepts.technical: For stride-1 k × k convs stacked L times: 1 + L(k − 1). A stride-2 pooling doubles the step of every later layer.
concepts.significance: It quantifies the 3 × 3 → 7 × 7 claim on this page.
concepts.misconception: The book phrases this in terms of windows; the term 'receptive field' itself is added here for clarity.

concepts.name: Global average pooling
concepts.definition: Averages each channel over the entire spatial extent, turning (H, W, C) into (C,).
concepts.intuition: One number per feature: its average presence over the whole image.
concepts.technical: There are no parameters. In Listing 8.5 it maps (22, 22, 256) to (256,).
concepts.significance: It connects the conv stack to the Dense classifier; the authors return to the problem of averaging such a large map on p.265.
concepts.misconception: It is not a small-window downsampling like MaxPooling2D; it collapses all spatial positions at once.

code.title: An incorrectly structured ConvNet missing its max-pooling layers
code.original_code:
inputs = keras.Input(shape=(28, 28, 1))
x = layers.Conv2D(filters=64, kernel_size=3, activation="relu")(inputs)
x = layers.Conv2D(filters=128, kernel_size=3, activation="relu")(x)
x = layers.Conv2D(filters=256, kernel_size=3, activation="relu")(x)
x = layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(x)
outputs = layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")(x)
model_no_max_pool = keras.Model(inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs)

deeper.title: Checking 7 × 7 step by step
deeper.body:
1. A unit in conv layer 1 sees a 3 × 3 input patch.
2. A unit in layer 2 sees a 3 × 3 patch of layer-1 units. Neighbouring layer-1 units are offset by one input pixel, so together they cover 3 + 2 = 5 input pixels per side.
3. Layer 3 adds 2 more: 7 × 7.

Now insert a 2 × 2 stride-2 max pool after layer 1. Layer-1 receptive field: 3. Pool: 3 + 1 = 4, and the step between neighbouring units becomes 2 pixels. A 3 × 3 conv after the pool then adds (3 − 1)·2 = 4, giving 8. Each further pool doubles the step, so the receptive field grows geometrically. This calculation is an addition to the book; it makes the authors' point precise.

deeper.title: Max pooling as a 'was it here?' summary
deeper.body: Imagine scanning a page for the letter 'e' and reporting one number per 2 × 2 block of words: the best match in the block. You lose the exact position within the block but keep whether and how strongly it occurred. That is what max pooling keeps from a feature map. The book develops this on p.265 (maximal presence vs. average presence).

deeper.title: Cost comparison
deeper.body: Multiply–accumulate operations for the third conv layer here: 22·22 positions × (3·3·128) inputs × 256 filters ≈ 142.7 M. Without pooling, the expensive late layers run at nearly full resolution. Pooling cuts the number of positions by 4× per stage. (Arithmetic added here, not from the book.)

misconceptions.claim: Max pooling has learnable weights, like a small convolution.
misconceptions.correction: The page says patches are transformed by a hardcoded max operation; pooling layers have 0 parameters.

misconceptions.claim: Removing pooling makes the model much bigger in parameters.
misconceptions.correction: Parameter count depends on kernel and channel sizes, not on feature-map size. What grows is computation and the size of the final map, and receptive fields stay small.

misconceptions.claim: Max pooling takes the max across channels.
misconceptions.correction: It takes the max of each channel separately over a spatial window; the channel count is unchanged.

misconceptions.claim: Deeper layers automatically see the whole image.
misconceptions.correction: With stride-1 3 × 3 convs, the third layer sees only 7 × 7 input pixels.

earlier.note: Start of 8.1.2: max pooling halves 26 × 26 to 13 × 13; strides and padding introduced just before.
The first ConvNet example alternating Conv2D and MaxPooling2D, and the idea that ConvNets learn spatial hierarchies.

later.note: The rest of the critique: 7 × 7 windows are too small; averaging a 22 × 22 map destroys information; why max beats average pooling and strides.
The cats-vs-dogs model again alternates Conv2D and MaxPooling2D, reaching 7 × 7 before GlobalAveragePooling2D.
Segmentation models use strided convolutions instead of max pooling to retain location information.
ConvNet design principles: blocks of convolutions followed by max pooling, filters increase as spatial size decreases.

takeaways: Max pooling outputs, per channel, the maximum over each window. It is a hardcoded operation with no weights, unlike convolution's learned kernel.
Usual settings: pooling uses 2 × 2 windows with stride 2 (halving resolution); convolution uses 3 × 3 windows with stride 1.
Listing 8.5 removes pooling: spatial size only shrinks 28 → 26 → 24 → 22, while there are still 372,234 parameters.
Without downsampling, three 3 × 3 conv layers see only a 7 × 7 patch of the input, so no meaningful spatial hierarchy forms.
Conv parameter count = k·k·C_in·C_out + C_out, independent of image size.

questions.question: According to the page, what is the key difference between how convolution and max pooling transform local patches?
options: Convolution uses a learned linear transformation; max pooling uses a hardcoded max operation
Convolution works per channel; max pooling mixes all channels
Max pooling uses 3 × 3 windows; convolution uses 2 × 2 windows
Max pooling has more trainable parameters than convolution
questions.answer: Convolution uses a learned linear transformation; max pooling uses a hardcoded max operation
questions.explanation: The page says exactly this. The second option is reversed: convolution mixes channels and pooling is per channel. The window sizes are swapped in the third option. Pooling has zero parameters.

questions.question: Verify the parameter count 73,856 for conv2d_4 in the summary.
questions.explanation: Each of the 128 filters has a 3 × 3 × 64 kernel (64 input channels from the previous layer) plus one bias.

questions.question: Why does the spatial size go 28 → 26 → 24 → 22 in Listing 8.5?
questions.answer: Each 3 × 3 convolution uses valid padding (the default) and stride 1, so it loses one pixel on each border: output = input − 3 + 1.
questions.explanation: There is no pooling or stride, so the border effect described on p.262-263 is the only source of shrinkage.

questions.question: Explain why the third layer's 3 × 3 windows correspond to 7 × 7 windows in the input, and why that is a problem for classifying digits.
questions.answer: Each stride-1 3 × 3 layer expands the region of input seen by 2 pixels (3 → 5 → 7). A 7 × 7 patch is a small fraction of a 28 × 28 digit, so even the last layer's features are local and cannot encode the digit's global shape.
questions.explanation: The book makes this point as the first of two problems (continued on p.265). Downsampling lets receptive fields grow much faster.

questions.question: A feature map of shape (26, 26, 64) passes through MaxPooling2D with 2 × 2 windows and stride 2. What is the output shape?
questions.explanation: Height and width are halved; max pooling works per channel, so the channel count stays 64. (13, 13, 32) wrongly halves channels, (24, 24, 64) is what a 3 × 3 valid convolution would give, and (26, 26, 16) confuses pooling with channel reduction.

questions.question: Removing the max-pooling layers did not cause a parameter explosion here (372,234 parameters). So what is the real cost of omitting them?
questions.answer: The cost is architectural and computational. Receptive fields stay tiny (no spatial hierarchy), the final feature map is large (22 × 22), so global averaging throws away a lot of information, and every late layer computes over many more positions.
questions.explanation: Conv parameters don't depend on spatial size. The two problems named by the book (p.264-265) are about hierarchy and the information carried by the final map.

questions.question: Without looking, can you compute every row of the summary table (shape and Param #) from Listing 8.5 alone?
questions.explanation: If you can, you understand valid convolutions, weight sharing and global pooling.
